say.text: Welcome to your very first class! I'll assume you know nothing yet, and that's perfect. Nothing is graded today. Just listen, and say each word back to me. Tap Next whenever you're ready, and tap any word to hear it again.
French uses the same alphabet as English, but the letters have French names. Tap any letter to hear it.
French has two sounds English mixes up. Ou sounds like oo in food. U is new: round your lips for oo, and say ee. Listen to tu, you, and tout, all.
When a vowel comes before n or m at the end of a syllable, it's nasal: the air goes through your nose and you don't say the n. Listen to bon, good.

day1.title: The French r and silent letters

say.text: The French r is made at the back of the throat, a little like gargling softly. And most letters at the end of a word are silent: petit sounds like puh-tee.
French accents change the sound. É, with an acute accent, sounds like ay in day. È and ê are like e in bed. The little hook under ç makes it sound like s.
Now your first greeting: bonjour, hello. Listen, and say it back to me.

body.text: French needs a little word before food and drink even where English has none: du pain (some bread), de l'eau (some water).
Du is for masculine nouns, de la for feminine ones, and de l' before a vowel.

why.text: French has no single word for 'some', so it combines de with the article (du, de la, des) to say 'part of' something you can't count.

rules.title: Le and la: every noun is masculine or feminine

"My" changes too: mon for masculine, ma for feminine. Learn each noun with its le or la.

why.text: French nouns are grouped as masculine or feminine, a habit kept from Latin. The article (le, la, un, une) shows which group, so learn each noun with it.

rules.title: Culture: greetings in the French-speaking world

body.text: Always start with "Bonjour" (plus "madame" or "monsieur"): in a shop, to a bus driver, before asking anything. Skipping it is the classic mistake that makes people seem rude.
La bise: usually two kisses in most of France, three or even four in some regions, one in Belgium, three in Switzerland. In Québec people kiss less often, and hugs are common.
Gestures: pulling down your lower eyelid ("mon œil !") means "I don't believe you". A shrug with "bof" means "meh". When counting, the French start with the thumb.
In West Africa, greetings take time: ask about the family and the day before getting to business, and shake hands with your right hand.

why.text: La bise, kisses on the cheek, shows warmth, and each region has its own count, so watching locals helps.

body.text: To say you want to do something, put the verb in its dictionary form (ending in -er, -ir or -re) after je veux.
On is a very common way to say "we": on mange (we're eating).

why.text: Vouloir takes another verb in its plain form (the infinitive) right after it, just like English 'want to'.

body.text: French wraps the verb in two words: ne before it, pas after it. Ne becomes n' before a vowel: je n'ai pas.
After pas, "a" and "some" become de: je n'ai pas de frère (I don't have a brother).

why.text: Ne … pas wraps around the verb. Ne was the original 'not'; pas, 'a step', was added for emphasis long ago and became part of every negative.

body.text: When you talk about liking things in general, French keeps le, la or les: j'aime le chocolat, tu aimes les chiens ?
J'adore is stronger than j'aime.

why.text: In French a noun usually needs an article. When you talk about things in general, like what you love, you use le, la or les.

rules.title: Three ways to ask a question

body.text: In conversation, just raise your voice at the end: tu as quel âge ?
Est-ce que at the start also turns a sentence into a question, and qu'est-ce que means "what". Swapping the verb and subject (comment allez-vous ?) is more formal.

why.text: French has a formal and a casual way to ask: rising intonation in speech, est-ce que in everyday talk, and swapping the verb and subject in formal French.

rules.title: À for cities, en / au for countries

body.text: Use à with cities: j'habite à Lyon.
With countries, use en for feminine ones (en France), au for masculine ones (au Canada) and aux for plural ones (aux États-Unis). "From" is de, du or des: je viens des États-Unis.

why.text: French uses à for cities, and en or au for countries depending on the country's gender, because the little word has to match it.

rules.title: The past: j'ai mangé, je suis allé

body.text: The everyday past (passé composé) is avoir + the past participle: j'ai mangé, j'ai regardé.

rules.title: Culture: at the table in French

body.text: In France, lunch is around noon to 2 and dinner around 8. In Québec, Belgium and Switzerland the meals are "déjeuner, dîner, souper": breakfast, lunch, dinner. So "dîner" there is lunch!
Keep your hands on the table (wrists resting on the edge), not in your lap. Bread goes on the tablecloth next to your plate.
Tap water is free: ask for "une carafe d'eau". Service is included in French prices ("service compris"), so a tip is kind but optional. In Québec, tip about 15%.

why.text: Meals are long and social in France, so rules like keeping hands on the table and waiting before eating show respect.

rules.title: Two past tenses: the scene and the event

body.text: The imparfait sets the scene: what was going on or used to happen (elle habitait, elle allait). The passé composé tells the event (elle a trouvé).
Fairy tales use a literary past you'll only read: ils vécurent (they lived).

why.text: French uses one past for the background (the imparfait: what was going on) and another for the events (the passé composé). Together they tell a story.

body.text: To say something had already happened before another past event, use the imparfait of avoir or être plus the participle: il était déjà parti (he had already left).
Pendant que (while) takes the imparfait for the longer action.

why.text: Avait or était plus a participle puts one past event before another, exactly like English 'had done'.

rules.title: J'ai mal à…: saying what hurts

body.text: Avoir mal à + the body part says where it hurts: j'ai mal à la tête (my head hurts). À + le contracts to au: j'ai mal au dos.
Depuis (since) with the present says how long: j'ai de la fièvre depuis hier.

why.text: French says what hurts with avoir mal à: literally 'to have pain at' a body part, so pain is something you have.

rules.title: Giving advice: tu devrais, à ta place, il faut que

body.text: Tu devrais + verb is "you should". À ta place ("in your place") and si j'étais toi ("if I were you") take the conditional: j'irais, je dirais.
After il faut que or c'est important que, the next verb goes into the subjunctive: tu dors becomes que tu dormes.

why.text: Advice is about what hasn't happened yet, so French uses the conditional (tu devrais) or the subjunctive after il faut que.

body.text: French people rarely talk about "dating" as a stage: you meet through friends, go for a drink (boire un verre), and things move on from there without much labeling.
Compliments tend to be understated and specific (ton style, ton sourire) rather than effusive. A simple "c'est gentil" is the natural thank-you.
Friends greet each other with la bise (a kiss on each cheek); a first meeting in a romantic context often starts with it too.

why.text: French dating tends to be less formal about labels, so things often grow naturally rather than through formal 'dates'.

rules.title: Culture: la séduction à la française

body.text: Flirting in France tends to be subtle and witty: a lingering conversation, a well-chosen compliment, a bit of humor, rather than big declarations.
Compliments about someone's style, laugh or taste land better than comments about their body.
Catcalling (le harcèlement de rue) is not charming and is actually an offense in France. Flirting happens in conversation, not from across the street.

why.text: In France, flirting is often about wit and conversation, so being clever and attentive counts for more than direct compliments.

False friends: for "I'm excited" say "j'ai hâte", because "je suis excité" can sound awkward. For "I'm full" say "je n'ai plus faim", not "je suis plein". A "librairie" is a bookshop; a library is a "bibliothèque".
Invited to dinner? Arriving 10 to 15 minutes late is polite, but be on time for work. Bring flowers or wine, but never chrysanthemums: they're for funerals.

rules.title: Je pense que… / Je ne pense pas que…

body.text: Je pense que (I think that) is followed by the normal present: je pense que tu as raison.
When you doubt or deny it, use the subjunctive: je ne pense pas que ce soit juste.

why.text: Je pense que states a belief, so the normal verb follows. Je ne pense pas que expresses doubt, and doubt calls for the subjunctive.

body.text: Vous is for strangers, older people, customers and anyone at work you don't know well. It's also the plural "you". Tu is for friends, family, children and people your age.
Wait for the other person to suggest tu: on peut se tutoyer ?

why.text: Tu is for family, friends and kids; vous for strangers, elders and work. Choosing one shows how close you are, so it carries meaning.

body.text: The conditional softens any request: pourriez-vous (could you), auriez-vous (would you have), je vous serais reconnaissant (I would be grateful).
Swapping the verb and subject (pourriez-vous) also sounds more formal than tu peux.

why.text: Wrapping a request in a conditional or a question leaves the other person room to say no, which is what makes it polite.

body.text: Texts are short and full of abbreviations: mdr (mort de rire, LOL), dsl (désolé, sorry), dispo (disponible, free), and the ne of ne…pas almost always disappears.
"Coucou" is the friendly hello for friends and dates. English loanwords like matcher, ghoster and le feeling are everyday app slang.
Splitting the bill (on partage) is common on dates, though some still offer to pay the first time.

why.text: Texting in France is short and full of abbreviations because speed matters more than spelling in a chat.

body.text: Teasing is often second degré (tongue-in-cheek): you say something with a straight face, and the other person knows you're joking.
A cheesy phrase d'accroche (pick-up line) only works if you obviously don't take it seriously. Laughing at it together is the point.
Keep teasing light and mutual; if they don't tease back, ease off.

why.text: French humor loves irony (second degré), saying the opposite of what you mean. Spotting it is part of understanding the joke.

rules.title: Culture: verlan, Québec and the Belgian numbers

body.text: Verlan flips the syllables of a word: fou becomes "ouf" (crazy), louche becomes "chelou" (shady, weird), bizarre becomes "zarbi".
In Québec, "c'est plate" means it's boring, a car is "un char" and "tiguidou" means everything's perfect.
Belgium and Switzerland say "septante" (70) and "nonante" (90), and parts of Switzerland say "huitante" (80), instead of France's soixante-dix and quatre-vingt-dix.
Keep slang for friends: "trop bien", "ouf" and "on y go" are perfect with them, not in a job interview.

why.text: French is spoken across many countries, each with its own slang and even its own numbers, so local words vary.

body.text: An idiom means something different from its words. Être dans la lune, 'to be on the moon', means to be daydreaming.
Learn each one as a block, with a situation. Change only the verb for the person.

table: Ça m'a coûté les yeux de la tête.

why.text: Idioms are pictures a language has kept for centuries. Their meaning comes from the picture, not the single words.

rules.title: How people really talk: dropping ne

body.text: In everyday speech the ne of ne … pas usually disappears: c'est pas cher, je sais pas, which often sounds like chais pas.
Tu also shrinks to t' before a vowel: t'as vu ?, t'inquiète. Keep the full forms for writing.

why.text: In fast speech, French drops sounds that carry no new meaning. Pas already says 'not', so ne often disappears.

rules.title: Telling a story: the linking words

body.text: En fait, 'actually', brings in the real story. Bref, 'anyway, in short', jumps to the point.
Et pour couronner le tout, 'and to top it all off', adds the last straw. Au final, 'in the end', wraps up.

why.text: These words tell the listener where the story is going, so they can follow along easily.

lines.text: Nous serions ravis que vous rejoigniez l'équipe. Nous vous proposons quarante-deux mille euros brut par an.

lines.text: Merci beaucoup, ça me fait très plaisir. Cependant, j'espérais plutôt autour de quarante-huit mille.

lines.text: Ça me semble raisonnable. On pourrait en reparler dans six mois ?
lines.en: That seems reasonable. Could we talk about it again in six months?

lines.text: Tout à fait. Nous l'inscrirons dans le contrat.

body.text: Meeting the parents usually means things are serious. Use vous with them until they suggest tu.
Bring a small gift (une petite attention): flowers, chocolates or a good dessert. Wine is fine, but some hosts already have it planned.
Sunday lunch can last for hours. Offering to help clear the table (débarrasser) is always appreciated.

why.text: Family meals are important in France, so being a polite, curious guest at the table makes a strong impression.

lines.text: Bienvenue ! On est ravis de vous rencontrer enfin.
lines.en: Welcome! We're delighted to finally meet you.

lines.text: Merci beaucoup pour l'invitation. Je vous ai apporté une tarte aux pommes.
lines.en: Thank you so much for the invitation. I've brought you an apple tart.

lines.text: Oh, il ne fallait pas ! Asseyez-vous, je vous en prie.

lines.text: Avec plaisir. Thomas m'a dit que vous étiez une excellente cuisinière.
lines.en: Gladly. Thomas told me you're an excellent cook.

lines.text: Il exagère toujours ! Alors, racontez-moi, comment vous êtes-vous rencontrés ?
lines.en: He always exaggerates! So, tell me, how did you two meet?

lines.text: Dans un cours de danse. Au début, j'étais nul, mais il a été très patient.
lines.en: In a dance class. At first I was hopeless, but he was very patient.

lines.text: C'est adorable ! Bon, à table, avant que le gratin refroidisse.
lines.en: That's adorable! Right, let's eat before the gratin gets cold.

body.text: Asking for someone's number (ton numéro) or suggesting a drink is perfectly normal. If they hesitate, take the hint gracefully.
A polite exit ("pas de souci, c'était sympa de discuter") keeps things friendly.
In texts, "bonjour toi" (morning, you) is a soft, affectionate opener.

why.text: Being clear and respectful avoids misunderstandings in a culture that values directness wrapped in good manners.

intro.text: These lines come up in the role-play “From opener to plan”. Hear them now, so you know them before it's your turn.

lines.text: Haha, ok : je parle trois langues, j'ai couru un marathon, et j'ai peur des pigeons.
lines.en: Haha, okay: I speak three languages, I ran a marathon, and I'm scared of pigeons.

lines.text: Hmm… je dirais que le marathon, c'est le mensonge. Les pigeons, ça fait peur.
lines.en: Hmm… I'd say the marathon is the lie. Pigeons are scary.

lines.text: Raté ! J'ai jamais couru plus de cinq kilomètres. À toi.
lines.en: Wrong! I've never run more than five kilometers. Your turn.

lines.text: Je préfère te le raconter en vrai. Un café samedi, ça te dit ?
lines.en: I'd rather tell you in person. Fancy a coffee on Saturday?

lines.text: J'adore l'idée. Seize heures, au canal Saint-Martin ?
lines.en: I love that idea. Four o'clock, by the Canal Saint-Martin?
